title: Beaded knot
subtitle: A French knot variation that holds a seed bead as it forms
excerpt: A beaded knot threads a seed bead onto the working thread before forming a standard French knot, so the bead sits at the centre of the knot with thread visible around it.
sourceNotes: Contemporary mixed-media embroidery practice. Combines French knot technique with bead attachment method.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small round glass bead with a central hole, used in bead embroidery. Size 11/0 is the standard for mixed-thread work.

heroPrompt: Several beaded knots on cream linen, small seed beads surrounded by tight thread wraps, close-up, natural light.

content.text: A beaded knot is a French knot with a
sitting at its centre. The bead slides down the thread before the wraps form around it, and the needle passes back through the bead hole rather than beside it, locking the bead in place.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 1 strand (must pass through bead hole twice)

items.label: Needle
items.value: Embroidery needle size 10 (fine enough to pass through the bead twice)

content.text: Thread the needle with one strand. Bring it up at the stitch point. Thread a seed bead onto the working thread and slide it down to the fabric.
Hold the bead in place with your fingertip. Wrap the thread twice around the needle, just above the bead.
Insert the needle back through the bead hole from top to bottom, going back into the fabric beside the starting hole.
Hold the bead steady as you pull through. The wraps tighten around the bead, holding it upright.

items.symptom: The bead falls off after stitching
items.cause: Thread did not pass through the bead hole on the return pass.
items.fix: Check the needle goes back through the bead, not beside it.

items.symptom: The thread breaks when pulling through
items.cause: Too many wraps for the bead hole size.
items.fix: Use only 1-2 wraps. The bead itself provides most of the bulk.

content.text: Beaded knots add texture and light to floral centres, fruit details, and scatter patterns. The same principle extends to more elaborate bead embroidery where beads are couched in rows or used to fill shapes.
